concepts.def: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols, so that any circuit can be read by anyone. The symbols needed are: open switch, closed switch, cell, battery, diode, resistor, variable resistor, LED, lamp, fuse, voltmeter, ammeter, thermistor and LDR. A cell is one long thin line beside one short thick line; a battery is two or more cells drawn in line. A resistor is a plain rectangle; a variable resistor is that rectangle with an arrow drawn diagonally across it. An ammeter is a circle containing A; a voltmeter is a circle containing V.

To draw a circuit diagram, components are joined by straight lines standing for connecting wires, with each component shown by its correct standard symbol. To interpret one, trace the loops: components on the same single loop are in series and carry the same current, while components on separate branches are in parallel. An ammeter is always drawn in the loop with the component whose current is being measured; a voltmeter is always drawn as a separate branch across the component.

For electrical charge to flow through a closed circuit the circuit must include a source of potential difference, such as a cell, a battery or a power supply. A complete loop on its own is not enough: with nothing to push the charges round, the current is zero. The source does not create the charges — they are already in the metal — it provides the potential difference that makes them drift one way.

Electric current is a flow of electrical charge. The size of the electric current is the rate of flow of electrical charge, that is, how much charge passes a point each second. It is not a flow of energy, and it is not the speed of the individual electrons, which drift very slowly even when the current is large.

concepts.term: Charge flow equation Q = I t
concepts.def: Charge flow, current and time are linked by the equation charge flow = current × time, written [Q = I t]. Rearranged, I = Q ÷ t and t = Q ÷ I. The time must be in seconds before it is substituted, so minutes and hours have to be converted first: 5.0 minutes is 300 s.
Charge flow, Q, is measured in coulombs, C. The coulomb is a quantity of charge, not a rate: one coulomb passes a point when a current of one ampere flows for one second.

Current, I, is measured in amperes, A; amp is acceptable for ampere. One ampere is a flow of one coulomb of charge each second, so the ampere measures a rate of flow of charge while the coulomb measures an amount of charge.

Time, t, is measured in seconds, s. Because the equations of this section are defined with time in seconds, any time given in minutes or hours must be converted before substitution: multiply minutes by 60 and hours by 3600.

concepts.term: Current in a single closed loop
concepts.def: A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop. Charge is not used up as it goes round, so an ammeter placed anywhere in that loop gives the same reading, whether it is before, between or after the components. What the components use is energy, not charge.

The current through a component depends on both the resistance of the component and the potential difference across it. Resistance opposes the flow of charge: the greater the resistance of the component, the smaller the current for a given pd across it. The current can therefore be changed either by changing the pd or by changing the resistance.

Potential difference, V, is measured in volts, V. It is the quantity that drives charge round a circuit, and it is measured across a component rather than through it. Questions are set using the term potential difference; a student who writes voltage instead gains credit, because voltage is an accepted alternative name for the same quantity.

Current, potential difference or resistance can be calculated using the equation potential difference = current × resistance, written [V = I R]. Rearranged, I = V ÷ R and R = V ÷ I. To find a resistance you divide the pd by the current; multiplying them instead is the commonest error in this topic.

Resistance, R, is measured in ohms, Ω. One ohm is the resistance of a component that has a pd of one volt across it when a current of one ampere passes through it, which follows directly from R = V ÷ I.

Circuit diagrams are used to set up and check appropriate circuits to investigate the factors affecting the resistance of electrical circuits. The standard arrangement puts an ammeter in the loop with the test component and a voltmeter across it; the resistance is then calculated from R = V ÷ I. The two factors investigated are the length of a wire at constant temperature, and combinations of resistors in series and parallel.

concepts.term: Resistance and the length of a wire
concepts.def: For a wire at constant temperature, resistance is directly proportional to length: doubling the length doubles the resistance, and a graph of resistance against length is a straight line through the origin. The temperature must be held constant, which is why the current is kept small and the circuit is switched off between readings — a wire that warms up has a higher resistance, which would spoil the pattern.

concepts.term: Resistors in series and in parallel
concepts.def: Resistors joined in series have a combined resistance larger than either one alone, because the charge must pass through both. Resistors joined in parallel have a combined resistance smaller than either one alone, because the charge now has more than one path to take; two identical resistors in parallel give half the resistance of one.

The current through an ohmic conductor at a constant temperature is directly proportional to the potential difference across the resistor, which means that the resistance remains constant as the current changes. Its I–V graph is a straight line through the origin. A fixed resistor kept at constant temperature is the standard example.

For some resistors the value of R remains constant, but in others it can change as the current changes. The resistance of components such as lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs is not constant; it changes with the current through the component. Their I–V graphs are therefore not straight lines through the origin.

The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases. A larger current heats the filament more, so its resistance rises and its I–V graph bends over into an S-shape, becoming less steep as the pd increases. A filament lamp is therefore not an ohmic conductor.

The current through a diode flows in one direction only. The diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction, so the reverse current is very nearly zero. In the forward direction it conducts, but only once the pd is large enough, so its I–V graph lies flat along the reverse side and then rises steeply forward.

The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases. This is the opposite of the behaviour of a metal wire, whose resistance rises when it is heated, and it is what makes the thermistor useful as a temperature sensor.

In a thermostat the thermistor senses the room temperature. When the room cools, the thermistor's resistance rises; the circuit detects that change and switches the heater on. When the room warms again the resistance falls and the heater is switched off, so the temperature is held near a set value. The same idea is used in fire alarms and in engine temperature sensors.

The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases. In bright light its resistance may be only a few hundred ohms; in darkness it can be millions of ohms. It is therefore used as a light sensor.

An LDR is used to switch lights on when it gets dark. As darkness falls, the light intensity on the LDR drops, so its resistance rises; the circuit senses that change and switches the street lamp on. At dawn the resistance falls again and the lamp is switched off. The same arrangement is used in automatic camera exposure and in burglar alarms.

To measure the resistance of a component, an ammeter is placed in the loop with the component so that it measures the current through it, and a voltmeter is placed across the component so that it measures the potential difference across it. The resistance is then calculated from R = V ÷ I. The circuit diagram is drawn using correct circuit symbols; a variable resistor or a variable power supply lets several pairs of readings be taken.

Graphs are used to explore whether circuit elements are linear or non-linear. A linear element gives a straight-line I–V graph through the origin and has constant resistance; a non-linear element gives a curve, and its resistance changes. The shape relates to the function of the component: the lamp's curve flattens because the filament heats up, and the diode's graph is flat on one side because it conducts one way only.

Circuit diagrams are used to construct appropriate circuits to investigate the I–V characteristics of a variety of circuit elements, including a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor at constant temperature. Readings of current and pd are taken over a range of values, including reversed ones, and plotted as I against V. The resistor must be kept at constant temperature so that heating does not change the resistance being measured.

mcqs.q: A circuit diagram shows a component drawn as a plain rectangle with an arrow across it at an angle. Which component is it?
options: a variable resistor, whose resistance is set by hand by moving a slider
an LDR, whose resistance falls when the light shining on it brightens
a thermistor, whose resistance changes when its temperature alters
a diode, which allows a current through it in one direction only
mcqs.explain: The standard symbol for a variable resistor is the resistor rectangle with an arrow drawn diagonally across it, showing a resistance that can be adjusted.

mcqs.q: A student is drawing a circuit diagram to measure the current through a lamp and the potential difference across it. Where should the two meters be drawn?
options: the voltmeter in the loop with the lamp, and the ammeter across it
the ammeter in the loop with the lamp and the voltmeter across it
both meters drawn in the loop, one on each side of the lamp
both meters drawn across the lamp, in parallel with each other
mcqs.explain: The charge to be counted must pass through the ammeter, so it goes in series; the voltmeter compares the potential at the lamp's two ends, so it goes across it.

mcqs.q: A closed loop of copper wire contains no cell and no power supply. Why is there no current in it?
options: the free electrons in the copper drift round on their own, making a current
a complete copper loop needs no cell, so a current flows round it
there is no source of potential difference to make the charge flow
copper has a resistance far too low for a current to be set up
mcqs.explain: The specification is explicit: for charge to flow through a closed circuit the circuit must include a source of potential difference.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the size of the electric current in a wire?
options: the total charge that has flowed since the circuit was switched on
the speed at which the individual electrons drift along the wire
the energy that the cell transfers to the wire in each second
the rate of flow of electrical charge past a given point in the wire
mcqs.explain: The specification defines the size of the electric current as the rate of flow of electrical charge, that is, the charge passing a point each second.

mcqs.q: A current of 0.40 A passes through a lamp for 5.0 minutes. Calculate the charge flow.
options: 2 C
mcqs.explain: Q = I t with the time converted to seconds: 5.0 minutes is 300 s, so Q = 0.40 × 300 = 120 C.

mcqs.q: In the equation Q = I t, which set of units is correct for the three quantities?
options: charge flow in amperes, current in coulombs, and time in seconds
charge flow in coulombs, current in amperes, time in seconds
charge flow in coulombs, current in amperes and time in minutes
charge flow in coulombs, current in coulombs, time in seconds
mcqs.explain: Exactly as the specification gives them: charge flow, Q, in coulombs, C; current, I, in amperes, A; time, t, in seconds, s.

mcqs.q: Two identical lamps are in series with a cell. An ammeter between the cell and the first lamp reads 0.30 A. It is then moved to a position between the two lamps. What does it read now?
options: less than 0.30 A, because the first lamp has used up some current
less than 0.30 A, because the meter is now further from the cell
0.30 A, because a current has the same value everywhere in one loop
more than 0.30 A, because it is now nearer the second lamp
mcqs.explain: A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop, so moving the ammeter within that loop cannot change its reading.

mcqs.q: A resistor in a circuit is replaced by one of greater resistance, and the potential difference across it is unchanged. What happens to the current through it?
options: it stays the same, because the cell always pushes out the same current
it stays the same, because the pd across the component is unchanged
it stays the same, because the cell alone decides the current
it decreases, because a greater resistance opposes the flow of charge
mcqs.explain: The greater the resistance of the component, the smaller the current for a given pd across it, which is I = V ÷ R.

mcqs.q: A potential difference of 6.0 V across a component produces a current of 0.25 A through it. Calculate the resistance of the component.
mcqs.explain: Rearranging V = I R gives R = V ÷ I = 6.0 ÷ 0.25 = 24 Ω, with resistance in ohms, Ω.

mcqs.q: A resistor of resistance 15 Ω has a potential difference of 3.0 V across it. Calculate the current through the resistor.
mcqs.explain: Rearranging V = I R gives I = V ÷ R = 3.0 ÷ 15 = 0.20 A, with current in amperes, A.

mcqs.q: In Required practical activity 3 a student doubles the length of nichrome wire in the circuit while keeping its temperature constant. What happens to the resistance of the wire?
options: it halves, because a longer wire gives the charge more room to move in
it is unchanged, since resistance depends only on the metal in use
it doubles, because resistance is proportional to the wire length
it falls to a quarter, because the longer wire gives even more room
mcqs.explain: At constant temperature the resistance of a wire is directly proportional to its length, so twice the length gives twice the resistance.

mcqs.q: A second resistor, identical to the first, is connected in parallel with it. What happens to the total resistance of the combination?
options: it doubles, because two resistors must resist more than one of them
it stays the same, since both resistors have the same resistance
it doubles, because the length of resistance wire has doubled
it halves, because the charge now has two separate paths to flow along
mcqs.explain: A parallel branch gives the charge an extra route, so the combined resistance is smaller than either resistor alone — here exactly half.

mcqs.q: In Required practical activity 3 a student wants to find the resistance of a length of wire. Which pair of measurements is needed?
options: the pd across the wire and the current in it
readings from a voltmeter in the loop and an ammeter
the pd across the wire and the charge that flows in it
the pd across the wire and the length of the wire
mcqs.explain: The ammeter gives I and the voltmeter gives V, and the resistance follows from R = V ÷ I.

mcqs.q: In the resistance practical, why is the voltmeter connected across the test wire rather than in the loop with it?
options: because a voltmeter in the loop would read the current in it instead
because it must compare the potentials at the two ends of the wire
because a voltmeter, like the ammeter, belongs in the loop
because pd flows through it, so the voltmeter sits in the loop
mcqs.explain: Potential difference is a difference between two points, so the meter must be connected to both ends of the component — across it.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the resistance of circuit components is correct?
options: R is a fixed property of every component, in the way that mass is fixed
R never changes, not even in a thermistor or an LDR
for some components R is constant, in others it changes with current
R only changes in components built to sense their surroundings
mcqs.explain: Exactly the distinction the specification draws: the value of R remains constant for some resistors but can change as the current changes in others.

mcqs.q: The I–V graph for a resistor at constant temperature is a straight line passing through the origin. What does this show?
options: the resistance rises steadily as the potential difference is increased
the resistance is equal to the gradient of the line at every point
the current does not depend on the resistor, since the cell fixes it
the current is directly proportional to the pd, so the resistance is constant
mcqs.explain: A straight line through the origin is what direct proportionality looks like, and it means R remains constant as the current changes.

mcqs.q: As the current through a filament lamp increases, what happens to the resistance of the lamp, and why?
options: it increases, because the filament becomes hotter
it stays constant, because the lamp is an ohmic conductor
it stays constant, because its I–V graph passes through the origin
it increases, because a bigger current always raises resistance
mcqs.explain: The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases, and a larger current heats it more.

mcqs.q: A diode is connected into a circuit the reverse way round. What is the current through it?
options: a tiny current, because the diode still leaks a little in reverse
almost zero, because the diode has a very high resistance in reverse
much smaller than the forward current, but still easy to measure
the same size as before, but now flowing the other way round
mcqs.explain: The current through a diode flows in one direction only, because the diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.

mcqs.q: A thermistor is taken out of a beaker of iced water and placed in a beaker of hot water. What happens to its resistance?
options: it increases, because heating any conductor raises its resistance
it stays the same, because resistance depends on the material only
it decreases, since a thermistor's resistance falls as it warms
it increases, because the warmer thermistor resists the current more
mcqs.explain: The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases, which is what makes it useful as a temperature sensor.

mcqs.q: A thermistor is used in a thermostat that switches a heater on when a room becomes too cold. What happens in the circuit as the room cools?
options: the thermistor's resistance falls, letting a larger current switch it on
the thermistor's resistance falls, so the heater stays switched off
the thermistor's resistance is unchanged, but the pd across it rises
the thermistor's resistance rises, and the circuit then switches the heater on
mcqs.explain: Resistance falls as temperature rises, so cooling raises it; the switching circuit responds to that rise by turning the heater on.

mcqs.q: The light shining on an LDR is made brighter. What happens to the resistance of the LDR?
options: it decreases as the light on it gets brighter
it increases, as there is more light for it to resist
it stays constant whatever the light level may be
it rises steadily as the light on it grows brighter
mcqs.explain: The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases, from millions of ohms in the dark to a few hundred in bright light.

mcqs.q: An LDR is part of a circuit that switches a street lamp on when it gets dark. What happens as darkness falls?
options: the LDR's resistance falls, so a bigger current can switch the lamp on
the LDR's resistance rises, and so the circuit switches the lamp on
the LDR's resistance falls, so the lamp is kept switched off
the LDR's resistance does not change, but the pd across it falls
mcqs.explain: Less light means a higher LDR resistance, and the switching circuit responds to that change by turning the street lamp on.

mcqs.q: Which circuit would let a student measure the resistance of a fixed resistor?
options: a voltmeter in the loop with an ammeter across the resistor
an ammeter and a voltmeter both in the loop with the resistor
an ammeter in the loop and a voltmeter across the resistor
a voltmeter across the cell with an ammeter across the resistor
mcqs.explain: The ammeter gives the current through the component and the voltmeter the pd across it, so R = V ÷ I can be calculated.

mcqs.q: A student plots I–V graphs for a fixed resistor at constant temperature and for a filament lamp. What do the two shapes tell her?
options: the resistor has the greater resistance, because its line is the steeper
both elements are linear, because in each of them the current rises as the pd rises
the lamp is linear with constant R, while the resistor's R falls as the current rises
the resistor is a linear element of constant R, while the lamp is non-linear and its R rises
mcqs.explain: A straight line through the origin means constant resistance; the lamp's curve flattens because the filament heats and its resistance rises.

mcqs.q: In Required practical activity 4 the resistor must be kept at a constant temperature. Why does this matter?
options: so that any change of resistance from heating cannot spoil the results
so that the resistor does not become hot enough to be dangerous to touch
so that the cell is not drained by the current passing through the wire
so that the ammeter and voltmeter readings are taken at the same time
mcqs.explain: The point of the investigation is the resistor's ohmic behaviour, which appears only if its temperature, and so its resistance, is held steady.

mcqs.q: A charge flow of 720 C passes through a component in 3.0 minutes. Calculate the current.
options: 4 A
mcqs.explain: I = Q ÷ t with t in seconds: 3.0 minutes is 180 s, so I = 720 ÷ 180 = 4 A.

mcqs.q: A current of 0.50 A passes through a 12 Ω resistor. Calculate the potential difference across the resistor.
mcqs.explain: V = I R = 0.50 × 12 = 6.0 V, with potential difference in volts, V.

mcqs.q: Which description matches the I–V graph of a filament lamp?
options: a straight line through the origin, in both directions
a straight line whose gradient rises with the pd
a curve that becomes steeper as the pd is increased
an S-shaped curve that flattens as the pd rises
mcqs.explain: The lamp's resistance rises as the filament heats, so the graph bends over and becomes less steep in both directions.

mcqs.q: A 3.0 Ω resistor and a 6.0 Ω resistor are connected in series. What is the total resistance of the combination?
options: it is 2.0 Ω, because the charge now divides between two paths
it is 9.0 Ω, because series resistances add together
it is 6.0 Ω, set by the larger of the two resistors
it is 4.5 Ω, the average of the two resistance values
mcqs.explain: Resistors in series are joined end to end, so the charge passes through both and their resistances add: 3.0 Ω + 6.0 Ω = 9.0 Ω, which is larger than either resistor alone.
